title: Agents and Tool-Use Systems
premise: Multi-step reliability is where demos die, and it is an arithmetic problem before it is a prompting problem. A step that succeeds 95% of the time succeeds 60% of the time across ten steps, and no amount of prompt tuning repeals that. This course starts from the arithmetic, spends most of its time on the two things that actually move it — narrower scope and better tool interfaces — and ends by attacking what you built.
laboratory: Career Side Quests is the centrepiece, because it is a deterministic multi-stage pipeline that already works. You will rebuild part of it as an autonomous agent and, most likely, make it worse. That is the point: the course's second outcome is choosing between workflow and agent, and the only honest way to learn that is to pay for the wrong choice once, on a system whose correct behaviour you already know.
scope_note: The red-teaming module targets systems you own and operate. Every attack in M6 is run against your own agent, on your own infrastructure, with your own data. Nothing in this course authorises testing anyone else's system.
sitting_rule: Every item is completable in one sitting. Nothing exceeds 180 minutes, and anything over 90 declares its own checkpoints.

panel.blind_note: Judges see the submission and the rubric, never each other's scores, and never the learner's self-assessment.
panel.disagreement: Scores are reported per judge and never averaged into a single number when the spread is 2 or more on any criterion.
panel.transcript_warning: Judges are instructed that an agent transcript reading as competent is not evidence the task was completed. Where a submission offers a transcript as evidence of success, the judge must look for the independent completion check instead, and score the criterion at 0 if there is none. This is the same failure the course teaches the learner to detect.

items.title: Building more effective AI agents
items.brief: The authors of the Building Effective Agents post on what they left out of it. Watch before reading the post itself.

items.title: Compounding error, on a system you own
items.brief: Career Side Quests is a multi-stage pipeline. Measure the per-stage success rate of each stage independently, on at least 30 real inputs. Then predict the end-to-end success rate from those numbers, and measure the actual end-to-end rate. Report both, and explain the gap in whichever direction it goes — stages are rarely independent, and the direction of the error tells you how they are coupled.

items.title: Rebuild a working pipeline as an agent, and lose
items.brief: Take one stage of Career Side Quests that currently works as deterministic code and rebuild it as an autonomous agent with tools and its own control flow. Evaluate both against the same gold set from AIE-102. Report accuracy, cost and latency for each. The expected result is that the agent is worse, slower and more expensive; if it wins, say so and explain what property of the task made it win.
checkpoints: both evaluated on the same gold set
accuracy, cost and latency reported for both

items.title: The decision rule
items.brief: Write the rule you would give a colleague for choosing between a workflow and an agent, derived from what you just measured rather than from the reading. Then apply it to three tasks in your own products and state the answer for each, including at least one where you expect the rule to be uncomfortable.

modules.title: Tool interfaces the model can actually use

items.title: Writing effective tools for AI agents
items.brief: The tool interface is the lever, not the prompt. Read alongside your own M4.5 result from AIE-101.

items.title: Model Context Protocol
items.locator: The specification: transports, then tools, resources and prompts.

items.title: SWE-agent: agent-computer interfaces
items.brief: The result worth carrying: changing the interface the agent acts through moved performance more than changing the model.

items.title: An agent over your own tools
items.brief: Build an agent over Carpark SG's real integrations — OneMap, data.gov.sg, HDB and URA rates — that answers compound questions a single lookup cannot, such as cheapest overnight parking within a radius given a stated arrival and departure. At least 15 labelled tasks. Report task completion, not step plausibility.

items.title: Tool documentation is the prompt
items.brief: Change only the tool descriptions — not the system prompt, not the model, not the code — and measure the effect on completion rate. Report the largest single-word or single-sentence change that moved it.

items.title: Retention: tool interface design for agents
tau-bench: tool-agent-user interaction
items.brief: The pass^k metric is the one to take away: run the same task k times and require every run to succeed. It is the metric a customer actually cares about, and it collapses far faster than pass@1 suggests.

items.title: pass^k on your own agent
items.brief: Run every task from M3.4 eight times. Report pass@1 and pass^8 — the fraction of tasks where all eight runs succeeded. Then answer the question a customer will ask: would you put this in front of their users, and at what pass^k would you change your answer?

items.title: Design against the decay
items.brief: Pick the single intervention you expect to most improve pass^8 — fewer steps, a narrower tool, a verification step, a deterministic fallback — and predict the improvement before implementing it. Then implement and measure. Report the prediction alongside the result whether or not you were right.
checkpoints: intervention chosen and improvement predicted in writing

items.title: Safe AI Agents and evidence-based AI policy
Indirect prompt injection in LLM-integrated applications
items.brief: Required before M6. Once a model reads untrusted content and can call tools, the content is an instruction channel you did not intend to expose.

items.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
items.locator: All ten entries once; then re-read the four that apply to a tool-using agent.

items.title: Least privilege, enforced rather than requested
items.brief: Your M3.4 agent has tool access. Constrain it so the limits hold even when the model tries to exceed them: scoped credentials, an allowlist enforced outside the model, rate and spend caps, and no destructive capability it does not need. Then demonstrate enforcement by instructing the agent directly to exceed each limit and showing that it cannot.
checkpoints: each limit demonstrated to hold under direct instruction

items.title: Personal data in AI systems, per the local regulator
items.locator: The sections on lawful basis for using personal data, and on measures expected when deploying.

items.title: What leaks
items.brief: For one product, trace every piece of personal data that reaches a model: what it is, which provider receives it, whether it leaves Singapore, how long it is retained, and whether a user could ask you to delete it and be told the truth. Then find the leak you did not intend - a system prompt echoed back, another user's data surviving in a shared cache, an error message carrying a payload. Report what you found and what you changed.
checkpoints: one unintended exposure found and fixed

items.title: Retention: privilege boundaries for tool-using models
Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
Make it do the thing it must not
items.brief: Against your own agent only. Write down three things it must never do, then try to make it do each. Include at least one indirect injection — content the agent retrieves rather than input you type — because that is the channel your sandboxing in M5.4 was supposed to close. Report every attack attempted, including the ones that failed, and what the successful ones reveal about where trust was misplaced.
checkpoints: three prohibited behaviours stated in advance

items.title: The disclosure
items.brief: Write what you would tell a customer about the residual risk in this agent — the honest version, including what you could not close and what you would need in order to close it. This is the document a solutions engineer actually has to produce, and the one most people cannot write without either alarming or misleading the reader.

items.title: Retention: attack surface of a tool-using agent
inspect_ai: agent scorers and solvers
items.locator: The solver and agent modules. The scorer protocol was read in AIE-102 M3.5 — start from what an agent solver adds on top of it rather than from the beginning.

items.title: Task completion, not transcript plausibility
items.brief: Build an eval harness for your agent where success is determined by checking world state — the record was created, the number is correct, the file exists — and never by reading the agent's own account of what it did. Run it over the M3.4 tasks and compare the result against what a judge scoring the transcripts alone would have concluded. The gap between those two numbers is the deliverable. Extend the eval suite you already wired into CI in AIE-102 M6.4 rather than standing up a second one — the state checks are new, the harness is not.

items.title: The plausible failure
items.brief: Find one run where the transcript reads as a complete success and the task was not completed. Quote the passage that fooled you and explain what made it convincing.

items.title: Retention: agent evaluation and state-based scoring
How we built our multi-agent research system
items.brief: A production multi-agent system described by the people who shipped it, including the token cost multiple and the tasks where it did not pay.

items.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
items.brief: A failure taxonomy built from real traces. Read before building one, not after.

items.title: Two agents, and prove it was worth it
items.brief: Build a multi-agent version of a task you already solved with one agent - a genuine division of labour, not one agent with a second rubber-stamping it. Evaluate both on the same task set for completion rate, pass^k, token cost and wall-clock. Multi-agent systems routinely cost several times the tokens for no reliability gain; if that is what you measure, that is the finding and it earns full credit. Then classify every failure against the taxonomy from M8.2, and name any failure the taxonomy does not cover.
checkpoints: single-agent baseline re-run on the same set

items.title: Retention: multi-agent designs and their failure modes
Ship an agent that knows its own limits
items.brief: Put an agent into one of your live products, publicly reachable, with enforced privilege limits and a deterministic fallback for the cases where it should not be trusted. The scope must be narrow enough that its measured pass^k is defensible.

items.title: The reliability report
items.brief: Report pass@1 and pass^k, the residual risks from M6, the workflow-versus-agent decision and why it went the way it did, and the tasks you deliberately excluded from scope. The excluded list is the part a reader will trust you for.

items.title: Publish
items.brief: Publish this as the next chapter of your public engineering log — one growing site, not a sixth standalone post. The chapter must stand alone on its own page for a reader arriving cold, and must connect backwards to at least one result from an earlier chapter. Publish at a stable public URL with the eval harness reachable.

items.title: Oral defense
items.brief: Three unscripted questions generated from your report at defense time, answered aloud without notes.
sample_question_shapes: Your pass^8 is X. A customer wants this handling their billing queries. What do you tell them?
You closed two of three attacks. Talk me through the one you did not.
Where would this agent fail in a way your eval would not catch?

rubrics.anti_gaming: A result showing multi-agent was not worth it scores full marks. Judges are told the fashionable conclusion is not the graded one, and that a submission reporting a win must show the single-agent baseline was iterated as hard as the multi-agent version.

completion.required: All assignments and the project submitted. Readings and lectures are tier 0 and are tracked but never counted toward mastery.
completion.grade_rollup: Deterministic. Each item's tier sets its weight; panel scores enter as per-criterion values; nothing is rounded up. Computed in TypeScript, never by a model.
completion.mastery_note: Sets initial mastery on the six agent skills, including red-teaming. FSRS then decays them, so the transcript reports what is currently held.

multi_agent_note: Multi-agent arrives last and deliberately. It is the architecture people reach for first and justify least, and the only honest way to evaluate it is against a single-agent baseline you have already measured - which is what the previous seven modules were for.
